one_line: Yard- and gate-mounted vision (plus driver phone-photo verification) that turns pre/post-trip inspection photos, seal numbers and trailer movements into audit-ready evidence for 5-50 power-unit fleets in Middlesex County, NJ.

problem.summary: Federal rules give a small interstate carrier two separate inspection duties that both live on paper today. Before driving, no CMV may be operated unless the driver is satisfied the listed parts and accessories are in good working order (49 CFR 392.7(a)); at the end of each day's work the driver must additionally prepare a report on each vehicle operated covering 11 parts and accessories - but only where a defect or deficiency is discovered, and not for intermodal equipment tendered by an intermodal equipment provider (49 CFR 396.11(a)). The report, the repair certification and the next driver's review certification must be kept three months, and the carrier must certify repairs before dispatch (396.11(a)(3)-(4), 396.13). In practice the daily walkaround and any resulting report are a clipboard-and-text-message workflow (inference from the site visits and vendor positioning described below, not from a measured survey): photos sit on drivers' personal phones, trailer condition is discovered at the customer's dock, and the fleet has no defensible record when a roadside inspector finds a defect. About one in five vehicles inspected during the 2025 CVSA International Roadcheck - a three-day enforcement event, not a random sample of all roadside inspections - was placed out of service, with brakes and tires dominating. A one-year program in which CVSA-certified inspectors replaced driver walkarounds found defects on 1,000+ assets, 95% of them on trailers, and 59% of partners' trailers passed the stricter inspection versus 70% of the same partners' trailers passing a traditional driver DVIR; that is the vendor's own account of its own pilot, with no independent audit, and the two pass rates are not the same trailers, so treat it as directional evidence that driver walkarounds miss trailer defects rather than as a measured miss rate (inference).

evidence.fact: DVIR: every motor carrier must require, and every driver must prepare, a written report at the completion of each day's work on each vehicle operated, except for intermodal equipment tendered by an intermodal equipment provider; the report covers 11 parts/accessories (service brakes including trailer brake connections, parking brake, steering, lighting devices and reflectors, tires, horn, windshield wipers, rear vision mirrors, coupling devices, wheels and rims, emergency equipment). A report is not required if no defect or deficiency is discovered or reported; the driver signs; the carrier must repair and certify before further operation; report, repair certification and driver review certification are kept three months; the report may be created and maintained electronically under 49 CFR 390.32. Section (a)(5) exempts private motor carriers of passengers (nonbusiness), driveaway-towaway operations and carriers operating only one CMV.
evidence.year: 2026 (current CFR text; last amendment 91 FR 7896, Feb. 19 2026)

evidence.fact: Before driving, no CMV may be driven unless the driver is satisfied that the listed parts and accessories are in good working order; drivers taking intermodal equipment must inspect the listed components and be satisfied they are in good working order before operating over the road (49 CFR 392.7). This pre-trip duty applies independently of the DVIR and even where no defect report is required.

Before driving, the driver must be satisfied the vehicle is in safe operating condition, must review the last DVIR where one was required under 396.11(a)(2)(i), and must sign to acknowledge review and that repairs were certified; the signature requirement does not apply to listed defects on a towed unit no longer part of the combination (49 CFR 396.13).

Driver must inspect cargo and securement devices within the first 50 miles of a trip and re-examine whenever duty status changes, the vehicle has been driven 3 hours, or 150 miles, whichever comes first; the rule does not apply to a driver of a sealed vehicle ordered not to open it.

2025 CVSA International Roadcheck: 56,178 inspections over three days; 13,553 vehicle OOS violations; 10,148 vehicles placed out of service (18.1% OOS rate). Brake systems plus 20%-defective-brakes were 41.1% of vehicle OOS violations, tires 21.4%, lights 12.8%, cargo securement 11.4%.

Kodiak's own account of its CVSA Enhanced Inspections pilot with Drivewyze and Texas DPS (started April 2023): certified inspectors inspected over 1,000 autonomous tractors and partner trailers and found over 525 defects, 5% on tractors and 95% on trailers; 59% of partners' trailers passed the enhanced (zero-defect) inspection while 70% of trailers from the same partners passed a traditional driver DVIR; of 137 defects found in over 160 enhanced inspections of customer trailers, 46% were tire-related and 10% lights. A combination-vehicle enhanced inspection averaged 38 minutes versus 15-20 minutes for a properly performed driver pre-trip inspection. Vendor self-report, no independent audit.

Industry operating cost averaged $2.260 per mile in 2024; non-fuel marginal cost rose 3.6% to $1.779 per mile, the highest ATRI has recorded; truckload carriers averaged a -2.3% operating margin and empty miles averaged 16.7%.

Cargo theft hit record levels in 2024: 3,625 reported incidents in the US and Canada, up 27% from 2023; average reported value per theft $202,364 (up from $187,895); trailer burglaries and full trailer thefts remained elevated in major metros including the New York City area. These are CargoNet's own incident-intake figures from a company that also sells theft-prevention services.

Median pay for heavy and tractor-trailer truck drivers was $58,640 per year ($28.19/hour) in May 2025, with 2,221,200 jobs - the basis for valuing inspection and re-inspection time (inference: at about $28/hour, a 15-minute walkaround costs roughly $7 in driver time per inspection).

New Jersey requires all heavy-duty diesel vehicles 18,000 lb GVWR or more to pass an annual smoke-opacity emissions inspection at a licensed Diesel Private Inspection Facility within 90 days of registration or renewal - a second recurring inspection deadline on top of DVIRs.

buyers.size_where_it_matters: 2-50 power units; the DVIR duty starts at 2 units because carriers operating only one CMV are exempt from 396.11 (the pre-trip inspection duty in 392.7 still applies), and the economics start around 5 units and 3+ trailers
buyers.why: Recurring driver inspections on every unit, shared trailer pools they do not own, and direct roadside-inspection exposure; the national Roadcheck OOS data and the Kodiak trailer-defect findings both hit this segment hardest (the Kodiak split is directional - different inspection regimes, same partner fleet).

buyers.business_type: Specialized freight: flatbed, tank, auto transport, intermodal drayage
buyers.why: Cargo securement is a top-five vehicle OOS cause (11.4% of vehicle OOS violations in 2025) and securement photos are the evidence a carrier needs after a shift or a claim; drayage fleets also handle seals and the separate intermodal-equipment reporting duties in 396.11(b), which fall on the equipment provider rather than the driver.

buyers.business_type: Private fleets of wholesalers / distributors (grocery, beverage, building materials, foodservice)
buyers.why: Own yards and docks, seal discipline on deliveries, damage disputes with customers, and the same federal inspection/report duties once they operate CMVs in interstate commerce (inference: private fleets are in scope at the same 2+ CMV threshold, minus the one-CMV exemption).

buyers.size_where_it_matters: 20-200 staff, 1-5 buildings with a trailer yard
buyers.why: Trailer moves, gate logs, seal verification for inbound/outbound loads and detention disputes are daily operational questions; Middlesex County's freight profile counts more than 1,300 warehousing/distribution buildings (NJTPA, built on a 2010 baseline).

High vehicle count relative to staff, damage and 'pre-existing vs. new damage' disputes, and inspection practice that rarely goes beyond a checklist app (inference from the app-based products in existing_solutions; no local survey located).
Heavy stop-and-go duty cycles, frequent body and undercarriage damage, DOT-registered trucks, and inspection records that matter for insurance and roadside stops.

gap_for_local_installer: The incumbents sell per-vehicle SaaS plus their own hardware and cloud: Samsara, Motive and Lytx price per vehicle per month and want the whole stack; Whip Around and Fleetio are cheap apps that verify photos but have no physical presence at the yard; BlackBerry Radar tracks trailers but does not read seals or tie photos to DVIRs; UVeye is capital equipment aimed at large sites. Nobody in the 5-50 unit range sells a local, fixed-camera yard/gate system that (a) captures every trailer in/out event with plate and seal images, (b) attaches timestamped photo evidence to the customer's existing inspection and repair workflow, and (c) runs on-premises on a few hundred dollars of hardware with no per-vehicle fee. That is the opening: own the physical layer (cameras, gate, PoE/Wi-Fi, mounting, calibration, service) and be the integration layer rather than a competing dash-cam SaaS. (inference - the absence of such an offer is not something I could prove; it rests on the vendor pages opened above.)

technical_approach.established_pattern: Fixed cameras at the yard gate and at a marked inspection lane feed a local NVR/detector that (1) runs a YOLO-family detector for trucks, trailers, people and plates, (2) tracks objects across frames to emit entry/exit and dwell events per trailer, (3) applies zone rules (gate-in, gate-out, slot occupancy, inspection lane) to decide when to capture bursts of high-resolution stills, (4) runs OCR on plate, USDOT-number and seal-number crops, and (5) sends only low-confidence or exception crops to a small vision-language model for a plain-language second opinion queued for human review. The driver side is deliberately not a new app: drivers photograph the inspection items in whatever app the fleet already uses, and the yard system cross-checks that the unit actually arrived/departed and that the same trailer had no unrepaired defect flagged earlier.

models_and_tools.name: Ultralytics YOLO (YOLO family detectors)
models_and_tools.role: Real-time object detection/segmentation for trucks, trailers, wheels, people and light/reflector presence; runs on Jetson-class edge hardware. The repository license is AGPL-3.0, so a closed-source commercial deployment needs the vendor's enterprise license or careful separation of the model server.

models_and_tools.name: Frigate NVR
models_and_tools.role: Open-source local NVR built around real-time object detection with zones and tracking; all processing local, no cloud; integrates with Home Assistant/MQTT for event automation - a ready-made skeleton for the gate and slot event pipeline.

models_and_tools.name: PaddleOCR
models_and_tools.role: OCR toolkit for license plates, USDOT numbers on cab doors and trailer seal numbers; crop-level reads are queued for human confirmation when confidence is low.

models_and_tools.name: LFM2.5-VL-1.6B (Liquid AI)
models_and_tools.role: Small (1.6B) vision-language model with improved OCR and multi-image handling, 32k context, and a GGUF build for llama.cpp/CPU inference - used as the exception reviewer on cropped stills (for example 'mud flap missing or just shadow?') rather than as the primary detector.

models_and_tools.name: Qwen3-VL-2B-Instruct
models_and_tools.role: Alternative small VLM for the same exception-review role, giving a second vendor option if the 1.6B model's reading of dirty seals or low-light crops is insufficient.

models_and_tools.name: Cactus (cactus-compute)
models_and_tools.role: On-device inference runtime for phones; relevant if a driver-side photo-quality check ('is this actually a tire sidewall?') is later embedded in a customer's own app instead of running in the cloud.

hardware.item: NVIDIA Jetson Orin Nano Super Developer Kit (8GB, 67 INT8 TOPS, supports up to four cameras)
Ubiquiti UniFi G5 Bullet 2K PoE camera (gate and inspection-lane capture)
hardware.approx_cost: $129 single unit; $359 for a 3-pack (list price on the Ubiquiti store)

hardware.approx_cost: Unknown - no public list price was opened; distributor quote required (planning allowance is stated in the pilot section as an inference, not a cited figure)

technical_approach.fine_tuning_needed: Partial. The detector benefits from site-specific fine-tuning (500-2,000 labeled frames per fixed camera covering day, night, rain, snow, headlights and trailer-only views) because 'trailer with a missing light' versus 'shadow under a mud flap' is a local-context problem (inference from the detection literature pattern; no truck-specific benchmark was found). OCR needs domain adaptation to the actual seal and label stock the customer uses, but not a new model. The VLM does not need fine-tuning for v1 - prompt, cropped image and a confidence gate are enough - and should stay in a human-review loop; fine-tune a LoRA only if reviewers reject too many of its calls.
technical_approach.data_needed: Per camera: 500-2,000 labeled frames (truck, trailer, wheel, person, plate, seal) with night and wet-weather examples; 200-500 cropped seal and plate images with ground-truth strings; one month of gate-event ground truth (yard marshal log or manual count) to measure capture and OCR accuracy; historical inspection and repair records to calibrate what 'defect' means for that fleet. No personal data about drivers is needed for the yard half of the product.

measured_outcomes.finding: About one in five vehicles inspected during the 2025 Roadcheck was placed out of service (18.1%); brake systems plus 20%-defective-brakes accounted for 41.1% of vehicle OOS violations, tires 21.4%, lights 12.8%, cargo securement 11.4%.
measured_outcomes.sample: 56,178 commercial vehicle, driver and cargo inspections over three days; 10,148 vehicles placed out of service
measured_outcomes.study_type: industry (CVSA enforcement data, reproduced by trade press)

measured_outcomes.finding: Certified-inspector 'enhanced inspections' found over 525 defects on 1,000+ assets in a year, 95% of them on trailers; 59% of partners' trailers passed the enhanced inspection versus 70% of the same partners' trailers passing a traditional driver DVIR - directional evidence that driver walkarounds miss trailer defects. This is Kodiak's own blog about its own pilot; no independent audit, peer review or third-party verification.
measured_outcomes.sample: 1,000+ tractor and trailer assets inspected over roughly 12 months in Texas (vendor-reported)

measured_outcomes.finding: On-board video with instant driver feedback plus supervisor coaching was associated with roughly half the rate of overall risky driving behaviors (rate ratio 0.47, p<0.001), with no significant change in the control group (RR 0.93, p=0.44). The authors call the results preliminary; outcomes are vendor-coded risky-behavior events, not crashes.
measured_outcomes.sample: 158 on-board video systems across 7 business sites; about 237,000 usable trigger events
measured_outcomes.study_type: conference abstract (NIOSH NOIRS 2015, pp. 62-63; CDC Stacks lists Peer Reviewed: False)

measured_outcomes.finding: Driver approval of driver-facing cameras averaged 2.24 on a 0-10 scale among current users, but rose 87% when carriers used footage for specific proactive safety measures; insurers and attorneys preferred event-based over continuous recording and access limited to safety managers.

Even the best commercial multimodal model reached only 74.9% average accuracy on industrial anomaly-detection questions (MMAD; 39,672 questions over 8,366 images), which the authors call far short of industrial requirements - a direct warning against letting a VLM make accept/reject calls on vehicle condition unsupervised.

Cargo theft reached record volume with an average reported loss above $200,000 per incident and elevated trailer burglary / full-trailer theft in the New York metro area - the business case for seal photos and gate records. CargoNet is a commercial data provider and also sells theft-prevention services, so its own incident figures are not independently audited.
measured_outcomes.sample: 3,625 reported incidents in the US and Canada

legal_privacy.issue: DVIR content, signature, repair certification and retention
legal_privacy.rule_or_precedent: 49 CFR 396.11 requires a report at the completion of each day's work on each vehicle operated, covering 11 parts and accessories, signed by the driver, certified by the carrier that defects were repaired or repair was unnecessary, and kept three months; no report is required where no defect or deficiency is discovered, and intermodal equipment tendered by an intermodal equipment provider is handled under 396.11(b) instead. A camera system can supply evidence but cannot replace the driver's report or signature.

legal_privacy.issue: Pre-trip inspection duty independent of the report
legal_privacy.rule_or_precedent: 49 CFR 392.7(a) bars operating a CMV unless the driver is satisfied the listed parts and accessories are in good working order; 396.13 requires the driver to be satisfied the vehicle is in safe operating condition and to review and sign the prior report where one was required. These duties exist on days when no defect is found and no report is written, which is what a fixed-camera or photo-evidence system can actually support.

49 CFR 396.11(a)(6) expressly allows the DVIR to be created and maintained electronically in accordance with 49 CFR 390.32; the current CFR text reflects an amendment published at 91 FR 7896 (Feb. 19, 2026). 396.13(d) makes the same allowance for the driver review record.

49 CFR 392.9(b) requires the driver to inspect cargo and securement within the first 50 miles and re-examine at duty-status change, 3 hours or 150 miles, whichever comes first; the requirement does not apply to a driver of a sealed vehicle who has been ordered not to open it. A seal-photo product must not be presented as satisfying cargo inspection on sealed loads.

legal_privacy.issue: New Jersey notice rule for vehicle tracking devices
legal_privacy.rule_or_precedent: N.J.S.A. 34:6B-22 (P.L. 2021, c.449, approved January 2022) makes it a violation for an employer to knowingly use a tracking device in a vehicle used by an employee without written notice, with civil penalties up to $1,000 for a first violation and $2,500 for each subsequent violation. The definition covers devices used for the sole purpose of tracking movement (inference: a GPS/telematics unit plainly falls in scope; a fixed yard camera does not, but any in-vehicle tracking feature added later does).

legal_privacy.issue: Audio capture in the cab or at the gate
legal_privacy.rule_or_precedent: New Jersey's Wiretap Act permits a person who is a party to an oral communication, or who has one party's prior consent, to intercept it, unless the interception is used to commit a criminal or tortious act or another injurious act (N.J.S.A. 2A:156A-4(d)). Practical guidance (inference): ship the system with audio disabled by default and require a written policy if a customer insists on audio.

legal_privacy.issue: Notice for silent video surveillance of employees in New Jersey
legal_privacy.rule_or_precedent: I could not confirm any New Jersey statute requiring general notice or consent for silent video-only workplace surveillance. A secondary source says there is no such state statute; the NJ Attorney General's investigative-advice guide was not text-extractable for this question and the NJ Division of Consumer Affairs FAQ blocked automated access. Conservative practice is posted notice at the gate plus a written camera policy, which also supports defensibility if footage is used in discipline.

A1488 (2024-2025 session) would prohibit collecting biometric identifier information unless clear notice is posted at every common entryway, with civil penalties of $5,000 for a first offense and $10,000 for later offenses, and a fourth-degree crime for a pattern of violations; the text opened is the introduced version, not enacted law. Whether New Jersey currently has any biometric privacy statute in force is UNVERIFIED here - the source I opened is a bill text and says nothing about enactments, so treat 'no standalone statute' as an unconfirmed inference, not a finding. Design implication regardless (inference): no face recognition, driver identification or emotion analysis in the yard product.

legal_privacy.issue: Out-of-state biometric exposure from in-cab cameras
legal_privacy.rule_or_precedent: An Illinois BIPA class action against Lytx over dash cams using machine vision/AI to predict distracted driving settled for a $4,250,000 fund covering people who operated a Lytx DriveCam in Illinois between October 12, 2016 and January 1, 2025; Lytx denied wrongdoing. A New Jersey installer that resells or integrates face-analysing in-cab cameras can inherit that exposure for any driver working in Illinois.

public: FMCSA CSA/SMS Vehicle Maintenance BASIC percentile at or above the 80% intervention threshold, plus recent inspection history and OOS violations by carrier (public on csa.fmcsa.dot.gov) - the strongest public signal of a maintenance-documentation problem.

Fleet size and commodity from the carrier's MCS-150 (power units, drivers, for-hire vs private) via FMCSA/SAFER or an aggregator - target 2-50 power units and exclude one-truck owner-operators, who are exempt from the DVIR requirement (though not from the pre-trip inspection duty).

Number of terminals/yards and trailer count: multi-yard operators have the worst trailer visibility, and trailer-heavy fleets took the overwhelming share of defects in the Kodiak inspection program (vendor-reported).
Job postings for a 'DOT compliance clerk', 'safety manager' or 'yard jockey' - paperwork and yard chaos being solved with headcount.
Google/Yelp reviews of the carrier or its shipper customers mentioning late deliveries, damaged freight, missing seals or trailers arriving with defects.
Warehouse square footage and dock count from commercial real-estate listings - a proxy for trailer volume at that address.
NJ MVC diesel inspection deadlines and prior OSHA/FMCSA inspection or crash records as conversation openers, not accusations.
walk_in: Paper DVIR binders, clipboards or faxed inspection sheets in the dispatch office; drivers photographing damage on personal phones and texting it to dispatch.
No camera at the gate; a paper gate log or guard shack with a handwritten trailer sheet; trailer numbers written on the nose by hand.
Yard inventory mismatch: trailers parked with numbers not visible, unmarked trailer pool, no marked inspection lane and poor yard lighting.
Unrepaired visible defects in the yard - missing conspicuity tape, cracked lenses, hanging mud flaps, tires with obvious tread issues - while the fleet claims an inspection process.
Which ELD/DVIR app is on the dash tablet (Samsara, Motive, TruckX, Whip Around, paper) - determines whether we integrate or displace.
Seal discipline: where seals are stored, who records seal numbers, and whether outbound photos exist for high-value or food/pharma loads.
Shop bay condition and whether a tread-depth gauge or brake-stroke gauge is actually hanging in the bay versus on a shelf.

pilot.scope: 4-week pilot at one yard with a customer running 8-20 power units and at least 10 trailers: two cameras at the gate (in/out) plus one at a marked inspection lane; local Jetson-based processing; event records for every trailer arrival and departure with plate, USDOT and seal-number crops; automatic attachment of gate photos to that unit's inspection/defect record in the customer's existing app (Whip Around, Fleetio, or a CSV/webhook fallback); a daily exception queue reviewed by the customer's safety lead, not by us making pass/fail calls. No in-cab cameras and no audio in phase 1.
pilot.hardware: 3x Ubiquiti G5 Bullet PoE cameras ($129 each, or $359 for a 3-pack), 1x Jetson Orin Nano Super ($249), plus PoE switch, outdoor cabling, mounts, NVR storage and an LTE failover router (distributor quote; the planning allowance is in the cost range below and is an inference, not a primary price source).
pilot.success_metric: Capture rate of at least 95% of gate trailer movements against a manual yard-marshal log; plate/USDOT exact-match of at least 95% and seal-number exact-match of at least 90% on legible seals; at least 90% of inspection records for pilot units carry linked gate photo evidence; at least 70% of AI exception flags accepted by the safety lead on review (false-flag rate below 30%); zero trailers with an unrepaired flagged defect dispatched without a documented repair certification.
pilot.cost_range: Roughly $6,000-$12,000 for hardware, installation and pilot-specific integration, plus $250-$600/month for monitoring, model upkeep and support. Assumptions (inference, not quoted prices): 3 cameras at list price, 16-24 hours of installation at $100-150/hour, a $600-1,200 allowance for switch/cabling/mounts/NVR/LTE (no public list price opened), 40-80 hours of engineering to wire the event pipeline into one customer's app, and no new cabling trenching. The customer's existing DVIR app subscription is unchanged.
pilot.assumptions: Single yard with line-of-sight from two mounting points; power and network available at the gate; the customer already uses an electronic inspection/DVIR app with an API or export; seals are printed and legible; the customer names one accountable reviewer; the pilot reuses one calibrated detector build rather than requiring a fresh labeling round per site.

fit_score.rationale: Demand is real and regulation-driven but narrower than a simple 'nightly DVIR' story: carriers operating two or more CMVs must prepare a report at the end of each day's work, yet no report is required where no defect is found and intermodal equipment tendered by an IEP is excluded, so the durable hook is the always-on pre-trip satisfaction duty (392.7) plus the evidentiary record when a defect is found - hence 14 rather than 15. About one in five vehicles at the 2025 Roadcheck went out of service nationally, and the Kodiak pilot (vendor's own account, Low strength) found defects concentrated on trailers, which is where small fleets have least visibility. Local buyer density is strong: Middlesex County's freight profile counts more than 1,300 warehousing/distribution buildings, and New Jersey has roughly 50,000 FMCSA-registered carriers of which a bit over half report a single power unit and about 18,500 report 2-50 power units (statnorth's rendering of the self-reported FMCSA census; the page is behind a bot check so these counts were read from a search-engine rendering, not the live table). Ability to pay is the weak link: truckload operating margins were -2.3% in 2024, roughly half of the state's registered carriers are one-truck operations that are exempt from the DVIR requirement, and incumbents sell inspection apps at $4-10 per vehicle per month, so pricing must attach to avoided OOS events and cargo claims rather than software seats. Technical feasibility is medium: detection, tracking, zone rules and plate OCR are solved; tread depth, brake adjustment and crack detection from fixed cameras are not, and the best VLM scores about 75% on industrial anomaly questions, so the product must be evidence capture plus a human-review queue. Legal risk is scored 8/15, i.e. low-moderate rather than low: three of the four live constraints are design-avoidable for this pilot (no audio -> Wiretap exposure removed; no face analysis -> BIPA and the pending biometric bill removed; fixed yard cameras only -> N.J.S.A. 34:6B-22's vehicle-tracking notice duty not triggered), but the per-violation penalty statute binds the moment any in-vehicle tracking feature is sold, the state of NJ biometric law is unverified here, and the Lytx BIPA fund shows how large the tail is if that line is crossed. Defensibility is only fair: hardware is commodity and Samsara/Motive could bundle yard features, so the moat is local installation, calibration data, service response and integration with whichever app the fleet already runs.

risks: Incumbent bundling: Samsara advertises AI-assisted DVIR photo and location checks and Whip Around sells AI photo review as an add-on to a $5/asset/month plan, so a buyer may reasonably say the problem is already solved on the app side.

A narrower legal hook than the pitch implies: no DVIR is required when no defect is found and intermodal equipment tendered by an IEP is excluded (49 CFR 396.11(a)), so 'we make your mandatory nightly reports defensible' overstates the obligation; the honest pitch is pre-trip evidence plus repair trail.
Margin and price sensitivity: truckload operating margins were -2.3% in 2024 and non-fuel costs hit a record $1.779/mile, so a $6k-$12k pilot is a real decision for a 10-truck fleet.

Segment mismatch: roughly half of New Jersey's registered carriers report a single power unit (statnorth rendering of FMCSA census data) and are exempt from the DVIR requirement, and many have no yard to instrument - bad prospects who look like good ones on a carrier list.

Liability for missed defects: if an evidence system is quietly sold as a safety system, a customer will argue we should have caught the defect. Contracts and UI must keep the human reviewer and the driver's statutory inspection as the decision-makers.

False positives destroy adoption: ATRI found driver approval of in-cab cameras at 2.24/10, rising 87% only when footage is used for proactive safety - an over-flagging yard system will be ignored or disabled.

Privacy and audio: adding a microphone or face analysis converts a low-risk fixed-camera install into Wiretap Act and (for Illinois-operating drivers) BIPA exposure; the Lytx settlement shows the size of that tail.
New Jersey tracking-notice compliance: any in-vehicle tracking feature added later triggers written-notice duties under N.J.S.A. 34:6B-22 with per-violation penalties.

Site conditions: dirty lenses, headlights at night, snow and gravel yards will degrade OCR, and seal numbers are often illegible, so sell 'image evidence plus review', not 'automated seal verification'.

Data retention and breach: inspection records must be kept three months, but gate video should not be kept by default; an unclear retention policy on footage of drivers is both a privacy and a discovery risk.
Single-operator dependency: pilot economics assume one calibrated detector build reused across yards; if every site needs a fresh labeling round, gross margin collapses.
caveats: Local buyer counts come from a third-party aggregator of self-reported FMCSA census data (biz.statnorth.us/carriers/nj), which warns that fleet and driver counts can be out of date; that page sits behind a bot check, so the figures used here (about 50,000 active carriers, ~51.7% at one power unit, ~18,500 at 2-50 units) were read from a search-engine rendering rather than the live table and are treated as approximate. The Middlesex County warehouse figure (1,300+) is from the NJTPA Middlesex County freight profile, which is built on a 2010 baseline, not a current facility census. The out-of-service statistics are national Roadcheck results from a three-day enforcement event, not New Jersey or Middlesex-specific inspection data and not a random roadside sample. Prices from Samsara, Motive, Lytx, TruckX, BlackBerry Radar and UVeye are quote-based and no per-vehicle figure was verified from any source opened, so none is stated; the only public prices used are Whip Around's and Fleetio's published plan pages. No peer-reviewed truck-specific study of camera-based defect detection was found; the closest published work is industrial anomaly detection, whose best model reached 74.9%. The only camera/coaching study with numbers is a two-page NIOSH conference abstract that CDC Stacks marks not peer reviewed, so it is rated Low. Several numbers are explicitly inferences: per-inspection labour cost from the BLS median wage, the 2-50 unit carrier count from the fleet-size table, the pilot BOM and labour assumptions, and the reading of N.J.S.A. 34:6B-22 as covering telematics but not fixed yard cameras. Nothing here is legal advice; a New Jersey employment/privacy attorney should review the notice, policy and retention schedule before the first install.
data_gaps: cvsa.org returned HTTP 403; the 2025 Roadcheck figures were taken from Fleet Maintenance's reproduction of the CVSA release rather than the CVSA page itself.

No NJ-specific or Middlesex-County-specific inspection, OOS or crash data was located.

The statnorth New Jersey carrier page is behind a Cloudflare bot check and could not be read directly; its carrier-count and fleet-size figures were taken from a search-engine rendering of that page and should be re-checked against the FMCSA census before quoting them to a prospect.

No public price was found or verified for Samsara, Motive, Lytx, TruckX base plans, BlackBerry Radar per-unit bundles (the exact AWS Marketplace figure was not visible on the page I opened), UVeye, or the switch/cabling/NVR/LTE portion of the hardware bill.

Could not confirm any New Jersey statutory text requiring notice for silent video surveillance of employees (NJ Division of Consumer Affairs FAQ blocked automated access; NJ Attorney General guide PDF was not text-extractable).

Could not confirm whether New Jersey has any biometric privacy statute currently in force, and did not verify the status of A1488 beyond the introduced text; the 'no standalone statute' point is left as unverified rather than asserted.
Could not verify the New Jersey Data Privacy Act's treatment of employee and applicant data from primary text, so it is omitted from the legal findings rather than asserted from secondary summaries.

No peer-reviewed study measuring defect-detection accuracy of fixed-camera or photo-verification systems on commercial trucks was found; the Kodiak program used human certified inspectors, not cameras, and its report is a vendor blog post.
No measured crash-reduction figure attributable to cameras alone was verified; the studies found measure risky-driving events, not crashes.

Automated weigh-station and undercarriage-inspection deployments (thermal brake inspection in Texas, California virtual weigh stations) were identified only through search snippets and were not opened, so they are not cited.
Trailer-seal OCR accuracy on real-world dirty or damaged seals is unknown; no vendor or study benchmark was found.
